title: Refried Beans
subtitle: creamy fried beans, a classic side dish
excerpt: Tinned pinto or black beans cooked with onion, garlic, and cumin, then mashed in the pan until thick and creamy. They are cooked in fat, not actually fried twice. A simple side that goes with almost any Mexican meal.
sourceNotes: Refried beans are a staple of Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking. The name comes from the Spanish frijoles refritos, meaning well-fried beans, not fried twice as the English name suggests.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions. Reheat with a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and refrigerate for up to 4 days.

content.text: Mash the beans in the pan as they cook, adding liquid gradually. The finished texture should be thick and spreadable -- like a loose hummus. Keep the heat low so they do not catch and burn.

items.prepNote: use pinto beans or black beans (tinned, drained)

content.text: Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion for 6 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the garlic and cumin. Cook for 1 minute.
Add the beans and half the stock. Stir to coat the beans.
Mash the beans with a potato masher or the back of a spoon as they heat through. Add more stock to reach the texture you want.
Cook for 5 more minutes, stirring often, until thick and hot. Season and serve.

items.cause: Too little liquid or cooked too long
items.fix: Stir in more stock or water and cook briefly over low heat until loosened to your preferred consistency.

items.symptom: Beans catching on the base of the pan
items.fix: Keep the heat low and stir regularly. Add a splash of liquid if they start to stick.
Add salt after mashing and taste. Make sure the cumin fries in the oil for at least 30 seconds before the beans go in.

content.text: Refried beans are a staple across Mexico and the wider Latin American world. The name frijoles refritos means well-fried beans in Spanish, not twice-fried. They appear at every Mexican meal -- alongside eggs in the morning, with tacos at lunch, or as a side to grilled meat at dinner. The fat of choice has traditionally been lard, though oil is widely used today.
